newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Swedish 'No' not seen causing further EMU trouble.
newsitem.headline: Swedish 'No' not seen causing further EMU trouble.

text.p: Sweden's decision not to join the single currency early reflects public and political EU scepticism at home. But the move, which was no surprise, is not seen as causing further damage to economic and monetary union.

At first glance, Tuesday's announcement by the leadership of the ruling Social Democrats that Sweden will not join at the 1999 start may seem to be more bad news for Europe's EMU project, troubled by growing doubts about it's chances to succeed.

Germany's powerful Bundesbank has wrangled for the past week with the government over Bonn's plan to revalue gold reserves to boost public finances and France's new Socialist-led government has said it wants to renegotiate the EMU stability pact.

The uncertainty this has caused is seen on financial markets as boosting the chances of either a delay or of a relaxation in the entry criteria leading to the creation of a wide monetary union with most EU countries participating.

But Sweden -- a relative newcomer to the 15-nation European Union -- was never seen as likely to be in EMU from the start, even if it looks on course to meet key financial requirements for qualifying.

"Sweden, quite frankly, is a country whose entry or lack of entry pales in comparison to the importance of a country like Italy or Spain," said chief European economist Bruce Kasman at investment bank JP Morgan ahead .
"Anything the Swedish government does in terms of signalling its intent or lack of intent is going to have very little impact on the key issues here."

Senior European economist Michael Lewis at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London took a similar line ahead of Tuesday's decision. "Sweden is really a side issue. The market has got to decide if EMU is going ahead first of all. I think that is really depending on what is going in Germany and France."

But recent events may make it easier for Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson to defend a decision to stay out of the single currency launch on the grounds that it is better to wait because of the increased uncertainty.
"It makes it easier for Sweden to be outside if the euro is going to be weak," said senior economist Ian Gunner at Chase Manhattan.

"Now there are some doubts how financially stable it is going to be so it is maybe not as bad as it used to be to be outside EMU, especially with Sweden having made great advances in terms of stabilising their own public finances."
Lewis at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said: "Politicians' hands in those more sceptical countries have been strengthened by what is going on in Germany and France."
Sweden's Persson said reasons behind the decision not to join included a negative public opinion, while the EMU project itself was uncertain and shaky.
But he also said Sweden would join EMU when it was possible, and that it was not closing the door completely.

Tuesday's move, expected to be confirmed by the Social Democrat's party congress in September and then by parliament, also highlights wide differences in attitudes towards EMU between northern and southern EU member states.

While Sweden, Nordic neigbour Denmark, and Britain seem to have few problems in fulfilling key budgetary EMU criteria, a sceptical public limits their room for manoeuvre. Denmark and Britain are also likely to stay out from the start.
Meanwhile, the bloc's southern members Italy, Spain and Portugal are doing everything in their power to squeeze in.
A survey published by the European Commission last week showed more than half of the population in Britain, Denmark, Sweden and Finland against EMU. In contrast, 73 percent of Italians favoured it.
"In southern European countries EU integration is something positive," said one EU diplomat.
